articles.title: A Tennessee couple said nearly 30 years of mowing, gardening and holding yard sales gave them ownership of a strip next to their home; on October 29, an appeals court ruled that the developer owned the disputed land
articles.summary: Using a piece of land for decades can create a strong sense of ownership, especially when people regularly maintain it, plant gardens and use it for
articles.body: Using a piece of land for decades can create a strong sense of ownership, especially when people regularly maintain it, plant gardens and use it for everyday activities. However, long-term use does not automatically establish legal ownership. A Tennessee couple who claimed that a strip of land beside their home belonged to them after nearly 30 years of maintenance have lost their legal battle, with an appeals court ruling in favour of the developer.In its October 29, 2026, decision in Developed by Design, LLC v. James M Travis et al., available on Justia, the Tennessee Court of Appeals upheld a lower court's ruling that the disputed land belonged to the development company. The court found that James M Travis and his wife, Mary M Travis, had failed to establish ownership through adverse possession. Their activities, including mowing, gardening and holding yard sales, were not sufficient to satisfy the legal requirements.How the property dispute beganThe dispute involved Developed by Design, LLC, which had acquired approximately 43.39 acres of undeveloped land in Rhea County, Tennessee. The company planned to develop the property, which was located next to the Travises' home. The disagreement began in 2021 when James Travis objected to work being carried out near his property. He believed the company was crossing the boundary and interfering with land that his family had used for years. The developer maintained that the boundary shown in its property records was correct. It relied on a survey prepared by Jack B. Kimsey in 1966 and recorded in the Rhea County Register of Deeds in April 1967.On June 14, 2023, the company filed a lawsuit seeking to establish the correct boundary and confirm its rights to a 30-foot right-of-way across the Travises' property. It also requested an injunction preventing the couple from interfering with its use of the access route. The couple challenged the company's position and filed a counterclaim, arguing that they had acquired ownership of the disputed strip through adverse possession.Why the couple claimed ownershipJames Travis testified that his family had treated the disputed area as part of their property since purchasing their home in 1996. He described activities including mowing the grass, using weed trimmers, clearing walking paths, spreading gravel and maintaining a garden. They had also planted blueberry bushes, held yard sales and stored various belongings in the area.The couple argued that these activities demonstrated continuous and exclusive use of the land for more than the 20-year period required under Tennessee's common-law adverse possession principles. However, the development company disputed their claims. Its representative, Caleb Yawn, testified that he had observed a garden near the boundary but believed it was located on the Travises' side of the surveyed property line. Yawn also said that several objects, including a car door, kitchen sink, bicycle and old pipes, appeared in the disputed area after the disagreement began in 2021. He testified that, to his knowledge, the Travises had not begun mowing the disputed area until 2021. The trial court also questioned the credibility of James Travis's testimony concerning the couple's use of the disputed land.Why the appeals court rejected their claimUnder Tennessee law, adverse possession requires proof of actual, exclusive, adverse, continuous, open and notorious possession for the required period. The claim must be established through clear and convincing evidence. The appeals court found that the Travises had not satisfied these requirements. Although the couple had maintained and used the area, the judges concluded that mowing grass, gardening and planting bushes did not demonstrate the necessary degree of control over the property.The court also examined whether their use was sufficiently open and notorious. This means that the actual owner must have known about the possession or that the activities must have been visible enough to provide notice of the ownership claim. The couple had not installed fences or no-trespassing signs to indicate that they considered the disputed area exclusively theirs. Their daughter, Olivia Keller, also testified that there was nothing on the land indicating that it belonged to her parents.The court further found that the couple had not demonstrated exclusive possession against competing ownership claims. Regularly maintaining an area was not enough to establish that they had exercised legal control over it.Court upholds the developer's rightsJudge Thomas R. Frierson II delivered the appeals court's opinion, joined by Chief Judge Frank G Clement Jr. and Judge Steven W Maroney. The court affirmed the lower court's October 20, 2025, judgment in all respects. This confirmed the boundary line presented by Developed by Design and its right to use the 30-foot right-of-way. The case was remanded to the trial court for execution of the judgment and collection of costs. The appeals court also assessed the costs of the appeal against James and Mary Travis.The ruling highlights an important distinction in property law: using and maintaining land for decades does not automatically make someone its legal owner. A person claiming ownership through adverse possession must establish that their actions meet every legal requirement, rather than relying solely on the length of time they have used the property.You use AI every day. articles.title: China’s ‘Lipstick King’ touts AI tokens in first for Singles’ Day festival
articles.summary: The Singles’ Day shopping extravaganza in China unveiled a new attraction this year as it graduates beyond a long association with cut-price cosmetics and home appliances: computing credits used to access artificial intelligence tools.
articles.body: BEIJING — The Singles’ Day shopping extravaganza in China unveiled a new attraction this year as it graduates beyond a long association with cut-price cosmetics and home appliances: computing credits used to access artificial intelligence tools. The launch is the first time AI token packages have been offered as a significant consumer product category during Singles’ Day, the world’s largest shopping festival originally held on Nov. 11 each year. Top livestreamer Austin Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships of Alibaba’s QwenWork office AI service within half an hour during a Taobao Live broadcast on Monday, the company said. That is equivalent to about 2 trillion AI tokens, or units of text processed by AI models. “Chinese consumers are now very accustomed to using AI productivity tools,” said Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at the tech research firm Omdia. Frequent users can run short of credits, he added, which makes extensive purchases during a sales period “a very reasonable action.” It was unclear how much the token plans were discounted from normal prices, however. The livestream was the first sale of AI products by Li, who earned the “Lipstick King” moniker for amassing a huge following while selling vast volumes of lipstick online. It showcased QwenWork token plans, AI-enabled laptops and workplace devices. Chen Yusen, an Alibaba Group vice president and chief executive of QwenWork, also made an appearance. Li asked Chen whether AI could be used to build a digital avatar of himself to chat with fans around the clock. While AI could not replace Li, Chen responded, he hoped it could handle everyday tasks for users, freeing them to spend time with their families. Alibaba’s Tmall has launched an AI Token Center for the festival, offering consumer token packages from Alibaba Cloud, MiniMax, Moonshot AI and Z.AI, the e-commerce giant said. JD.com has also introduced an AI token section bringing together services from companies including DeepSeek, Z.AI and ByteDance’s Volcano Engine. Sales of AI token plans from Oct. 1 to Oct. 20 soared 450% from the previous month, Alibaba said, while sales of AI personal-computer laptops surged more than 300% year-on-year in the first hour of the Nov. 11 checkout period. Su said the tokens’ relatively long expiry periods could spur users to stock up, but warned that rapid changes in AI products may make consumers wary of prepaying for services at risk of being replaced or retired. Singles’ Day, which has run since 2009 in an effort to spur consumer spending, earned total revenue of 1.70 trillion yuan ($255 billion) across platforms last year, according to third-party data provider Syntun.

articles.title: Staffordshire's Alton Towers closes World of David Walliams
articles.summary: The closure comes following a "regular review of rides and attractions", Alton Towers says.
articles.body:
The World of David Walliams attraction at Alton Towers has permanently closed, the theme park has announced.

The park's creative team worked with Walliams and HarperCollins Children's Books over a number of years to develop the section of the resort, which opened in 2021.

"As we are no longer in the main season, guests are encouraged to check the Alton Towers Resort website and app for the latest attraction opening information ahead of their visit," the park said in a statement on its website.

Alton Towers says the closure comes as it regularly looks at "elements of our attraction offering".

It is understood the decision was made taking into account a range of operational and guest experience considerations.

Plans for future use of the area will be announced once they have been confirmed.

Among the rides in the Walliams-themed area of the park were Gangsta Granny: The Ride, a 360° special effects attraction, as well as Raj's Bouncy Bottom Burp, Royal Carousel and Flavio's Fabulous Fandango.

Walliams rose to fame in comedy sketch show Little Britain in the early 2000s alongside co-star Matt Lucas.

HarperCollins published his first children's book, The Boy in the Dress, in 2008.

He has since become one of the UK's most successful children's authors, having sold more than 60 million copies worldwide in 55 languages.

Some of his books, including Gangsta Granny and Billionaire Boy, have also been adapted into TV films.

He has published more than 40 books in total.

articles.title: Zombie skin cells may sound like a myth, but they can affect your complexion — here’s what derms say
articles.summary: Zombie skin cells, or senescent cells, can contribute to fine lines and loss of firmness. Dermatologists explain what causes them and how to treat them.
articles.body: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends (and questions) on our timelines, like how often you should be cleaning your makeup brushes. Zombie skin may sound like another TikTok beauty gimmick (or your next Halloween costume), but it’s actually a real thing that could be impacting your complexion. Zombie skin cells don’t die off like normal cells. Instead, they stop dividing and linger, releasing inflammatory signals that can damage healthy cells nearby. Over time, that buildup is thought to contribute to fine lines, loss of firmness and uneven tone. Everyone accumulates these cells with age, but certain things can speed them up. To learn more, I spoke with two board-certified dermatologists about what zombie skin cells are, what causes them and how to treat them. What are zombie skin cells? Zombie cells is a fitting nickname for this naturally-occurring process. “Zombie cells refers to skin cells that have entered a process called senescence, where they can no longer replicate but remain active in the body’s metabolic system,” says Dr. Sophia Reid, a dual board-certified physician in dermatology and obesity medicine and founder of Skin Secrets Dermatology, Aesthetics & Wellness in Park Ridge, New Jersey. “This is typically caused by aging or damage from UV exposure, radiation or other natural stressors.” To understand how these cells form, it helps to know how healthy cells normally behave. “Under normal circumstances, our cells divide, repair damage, die, and then are eventually cleared away via other cellular processes,” says Dr. Pearl Ugwu-Dike, a board-certified dermatologist based in New York City. But cells under significant stress can take a different path. “For certain cells experiencing significant stress from things like ultraviolet damage, oxidative stress, or even sometimes just the passage of time, they can enter a different state referred to as cellular senescence,” she says. “These cells go into stable cell cycle arrest. But they’re resistant to apoptosis, or the process of cellular death.” In other words, they stop working but don’t go away, and they don’t stay quiet either. “Some begin to release inflammatory molecules that can negatively influence the surrounding healthy cells,” says Ugwu-Dike. “I think of zombie cells as employees that have stopped doing their jobs but some of them keep sending disruptive emails to the rest of the office.” That disruption shows up on your face over time. “When senescent cells accumulate, they can release inflammatory proteins that can contribute to that breakdown of collagen and other structural proteins that help to keep the skin firm and resilient,” says Ugwu-Dike. “Of course, over time, that loss of collagen contributes to the visible signs of aging that we see, like fine lines, uneven texture and laxity or reduced elasticity.” Skin care products that can help with zombie skin cells “There isn’t a proven at-home treatment that effectively removes zombie cells from the skin,” says Reid. “However, maintaining a consistent routine and healthy skin barrier while being mindful of lifestyle habits that could further damage the skin is a great place to start.” According to the experts I spoke with, the below products can help keep your skin in good shape and mitigate the effects of zombie skin cells. Both Reid and Ugwu-Dike recommend using a retinoid because it can be particularly effective at stimulating collagen production that may otherwise be impacted by these zombie skin cells. Reid likes this lotion from Olay for patients trying retinol for the first time or those with sensitive skin. “It contains a gentle retinoid complex along with collagen peptides and aloe vera to address visible aging concerns without overwhelming the skin,” she says. It’s also fragrance-free, which is a plus for sensitive skin. To use, pump twice and smooth it onto your face and neck every night, then follow up with SPF the following morning, since retinoids can make skin more sensitive to the sun. If you’d prefer a serum, this one from CeraVe is another retinol option. “It combines retinol with hyaluronic acid, which provides a more soothing product,” says Ugwu-Dike. The formula uses retinol to help smooth fine lines and wrinkles and improve skin texture and radiance, while hyaluronic acid draws moisture into the skin. It also contains niacinamide, which helps calm skin, and three ceramides to help restore the skin barrier, a helpful combination since retinoids can be drying. The serum is fragrance-free, non-comedogenic and suitable for all skin types. “Ultraviolet radiation is one of the most established drivers of cellular damage and premature skin aging, so daily sunscreen is a must,” says Ugwu-Dike. “It’s also been demonstrated that photoaged skin has a higher burden of senescent cells than would be expected from chronologic age alone.” This sunscreen from Neutrogena comes recommended by Ugwu-Dike and protects against both aging UVA rays and burning UVB rays. It also absorbs quickly and leaves a lightweight, non-shiny finish that won’t feel greasy under makeup. It’s non-comedogenic, water-resistant for up to 80 minutes and can be used on your face and body. Ugwu-Dike also recommends adding a vitamin C serum to your routine. “Vitamin C is one of my favorite ingredients for addressing the visible effects of environmental skin aging because it helps neutralize reactive oxygen species and plays an essential role in collagen synthesis,” she says. She recommends this serum from Naturium, which also includes hyaluronic acid, glycerin and vitamin E to help hydrate skin. How to prevent zombie skin cells “Since senescence is a natural process, it cannot be avoided entirely but there are certainly ways to limit the impact of external stressors,” says Reid. Below, some of the ways the experts I spoke with suggest doing just that: Wear SPF: UV exposure is one of the biggest drivers of cellular damage that can push skin cells into senescence, so sunscreen is your first line of defense. Apply a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher every day, even when it’s cloudy or you’re mostly indoors, and reapply at least every two hours when you’re outside. Pairing sunscreen with protective clothing, hats and shade adds another layer of protection.Take care of your skin barrier: A healthy skin barrier helps protect against environmental stressors that can contribute to cellular damage. Use a gentle cleanser, moisturize daily and look for barrier-supporting ingredients like ceramides, hyaluronic acid and niacinamide to keep it in the best shape possible, according to the experts I spoke with. If you’re using active ingredients like retinoids, introduce them slowly to avoid irritation that can compromise the barrier.Focus on lifestyle habits: “Not smoking, and maintaining healthy living habits can help reduce cellular damage,” says Reid. That includes getting enough sleep, eating a balanced diet and managing stress, all of which support your skin’s overall health. Are some people more prone to zombie skin cells? Everyone accumulates senescent cells over time, but age is one of the biggest factors in how quickly they build up. “Older patients are more susceptible to zombie skin cells because our bodies become less efficient at clearing damaged cells as we age,” says Reid. Lifestyle factors matter, too: people with more cumulative sun exposure or who smoke may experience more of the cellular damage that leads to senescence. Your genes may also play a role. “Genetic differences in DNA repair and cellular stress response most likely play a factor, although data is still emerging,” says Ugwu-Dike. “People with certain chronic inflammatory conditions may also experience altered patterns of cellular senescence. But that relationship is quite complicated and remains an area of active research as well.” Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. articles.title: Death toll hits 31 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, with dozens still missing
articles.summary: Rescuers in southern Ukraine continued an intense search Tuesday for survivors at a bombed-out aid facility and shelter where at least 31 people were killed and dozens were still missing.
articles.body: Rescuers in southern Ukraine continued an intense search Tuesday for survivors at a bombed-out aid facility and shelter where at least 31 people were killed and dozens were still missing. Teams of emergency workers and volunteers picked through debris at the cratered blast site in Komyshuvakha, a village in Ukraine’s southern Zaporizhzhia region where bodies were pulled from the rubble and carried away in white plastic sheeting. More than 45 residents are still missing. “The scale of the tragedy is terrifying,” Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the region’s military administration, wrote in an online post. “This is one of the worst tragedies in terms of the number of civilian victims in our region since the start of the full-scale war.” As Ukraine prepared for a new round of U.S.-brokered peace negotiations next week, a wave of overnight strikes targeted power plants across the country, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people. Russia launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, triggering emergency power cuts, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an online post that noted the barrage coincided with U.S. elections. “The Russians think America won’t notice this signal of theirs,” he said. “But we need to notice and stop such terror. We need to help Ukraine defend its skies; otherwise, Russia will never stop its missile strikes.” Three days of mourning were declared in Zaporizhzhia, where Russian bunker-busting bombs, some filled with nearly 1.5 tons of explosives, were used in Monday’s attack. The dead included four police officers and two rescue workers, Semikin said Tuesday. At least five people were hurt. In the northeast region of Kharkiv, a combined Russian missile and drone attack wounded at least 62 people, local authorities said. A strike damaged a medical facility in the Nemyshlianskyi district, shattered windows in four apartment buildings and damaged cars. More than 200 patients were transferred to other medical facilities, Oleh Syniehubov, head of the regional military administration, said. In the Dnipro area, rescuers pulled a woman alive from the rubble Tuesday morning, after a Russian attack killed one person and wounded 17, local authorities said. The attack damaged an outpatient clinic and a hospital. Patients were transferred to other hospitals, Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said. Moscow kept up its nightly attacks on power plants and energy infrastructure ahead of winter, causing extensive damage and electricity outages as it carried out 20 strikes in 10 regions overnight, Ukraine’s energy ministry said. Ukrainian power utility DTEK said three of its power plants halted operations after significant damage from intense attacks. No injuries were reported. Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Tuesday that it had shot down 856 Ukrainian drones overnight. Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 493 drones were fired toward the Russian capital. A Ukrainian drone attack wounded two employees at an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, regional Gov. Mikhail Yevrayev said Tuesday. He added that there was damage to the refinery’s infrastructure. Rolling blackouts have been instituted in the south, west and east of Russian-occupied Crimea following attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow-installed officials said Tuesday. President Zelenskyy traveled to Germany Tuesday, beginning a new round of consultations with European leaders ahead of U.S.-mediated talks Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi to try and end the war. U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, confirmed the date of the talks late Monday, with negotiations to focus on postwar security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian efforts. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed Tuesday that a Russian delegation will attend the talks. Russia had agreed last month to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war, setting up the first such talks since February. The European Commission said it would host a meeting Wednesday with officials from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the European Union, NATO, Ukraine, the United States and the World Bank to discuss postwar reconstruction in Ukraine. Commission spokeswoman Paula Pinho did not comment on whether Zelenskyy would attend.

articles.title: Flights from UK airports among seven across Europe targeted by suspected bomb threats
articles.summary: Planes in Poland, Spain, Bulgaria and Italy have been checked for explosives following separate threats.
articles.body:
Seven passenger planes across Europe, two of which departed from the UK, have been inspected following a series of suspected bomb threats.

Two Ryanair flights, one originating from Dublin and the other from Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome following anonymous tips but no explosives were found, sources at the city's Fiumicino airport told the BBC.

The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian air force until landing.

Meanwhile, authorities have also searched planes in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria. It is unclear if the incidents are connected.

Aviation security expert Paul Mason said bomb threats on passenger planes "don't happen that frequently", which made the latest incidents "unusual".

"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told BBC 5 Live. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."

He said "there are a lot of processes" that the onboard crew and people on the ground must go through "to validate the credibility of the threat".

A flight may be asked to divert if the credibility of a threat "is of a certain level", Mason added, and in some cases the onboard crew may not even be advised on what the ground operators were dealing with.

In Rome, sources at Fiumicino airport told the BBC police bomb disposal experts carried out standard security protocols to ensure the safety of all passengers and crew.

Inspections of the passengers, luggage, and the aircraft yielded negative results, and the alert has since been cleared.

One plane which landed in Murcia, southern Spain - a Ryanair flight coming from Manchester - was also found not to have any explosives on board, Spanish authorities said.

One passenger later said she was unaware of the bomb threat until after the plane landed.

"We weren't told anything during the flight," Sarah told BBC 5 Live. "The plane stopped quite suddenly and then we were kept on the runway for around 30 minutes."

"Then the fire engines turned up, the bomb squad turned up and we were asked to evacuate," she continues.

Sarah said the plane had not been on the ground a minute before it was "surrounded by fire engines and police and a bomb squad". All the passengers were then escorted by police, leaving all their belongings.

"We were only later told that it was an actual threat, a bomb threat to the plane itself," she added.

Two flights heading to Warsaw were also affected, including one from London Heathrow.

The Heathrow flight was originally meant to land at the Polish capital's main airport, Chopin, but was diverted instead to the smaller Modlin airport, briefly forcing its closure.

A Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as planned.

Later on Tuesday, Bulgarian Transport Minister Georgi Peev said there were bomb threats against two planes travelling to the country's capital Sofia.

He told the state-owned Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) the flights were from the northern Italian city of Bergamo and Ireland's capital Dublin.

The flights into Sofia were not diverted and no explosives were found when the planes were checked, Peev said.

These incidents incidents come a day after a Wizz Air flight from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet, after a bomb threat.

Wizz Air said later that security checks had been made and nothing was found.

articles.title: US midterms: Trump repeats ‘total fraud’ claim over Alaska Senate race as America votes - top developments
articles.summary: Polling stations have opened in several US states as Americans vote in midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the final two years
articles.body: Polling stations have opened in several US states as Americans vote in midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the final two years of US president Donald Trump’s term.The elections will offer the first nationwide verdict on Trump’s second presidency, testing whether voters want to limit his power by handing Democrats control of one or both chambers of Congress, or keep Republicans in charge amid concerns over the cost of living and the US-led war with Iran.The results could also shape debates within both parties over the policies and messages that resonate with voters ahead of the 2028 presidential election.Trump repeats ‘total fraud’ claim over Alaska Senate raceTrump has again called the Alaska Senate race a "total fraud" in a phone interview with Fox News' Fox and Friends, referencing a New York Times report from last week that said Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Party helped recruit a "spoiler" candidate to appear on the ballot.The Trump administration recently stepped up investigations into the allegation that the candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan was recruited to confuse voters. Trump said the second Sullivan agreed "to participate absolutely illegally", adding, "It was a criminal act." He also claimed another person "who has nothing to do with politics" appeared on the ballot.Several Florida polling places shifted amid heavy rain, floodingPolling places in several Florida counties have been changed due to flash flooding. Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency in seven counties along the Atlantic seaboard that are being hit with flash flooding and extreme precipitation.NBC reported that at least four precincts in S. Lucie County, which Donald Trump won with 54% of the vote in 2024, had to be moved because of flooding concerns as the region is hit with “historic” levels of rain ahead of Election Day. Five polling locations in Brevard County also have been moved because of inclement weather and for the “safety and security” of election workers.DOJ deploys election monitors to 126 counties across USThe US Department of Justice (DOJ) has deployed around 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states, marking the first time the department has sent monitors to every state and what it described as the largest election-monitoring effort in its history.The department on Tuesday released a list of 126 counties where the monitors will be present, including several in states with closely watched midterm races.According to the DOJ, the monitors will observe polling places to ensure compliance with federal voting laws, including provisions prohibiting voter intimidation and discrimination based on race, colour, national origin or religion. Their remit also includes checking that voters with disabilities have a “full and equal” opportunity to cast their ballots and that polling places provide legally required language assistance.“We are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K Dhillon of the DOJ's Civil Rights Division said in a statement.The monitors are not law enforcement officials and are not involved in counting votes. They do not have access to voting machines or ballots, and are instructed not to interfere with the voting process. Their role is limited to observing polling places for potential violations of federal election laws, CNN reported.Midterms decide who controls CongressDemocrats need a net gain of four seats in both the House and Senate to overturn Republicans’ narrow majorities of 218-214 and 53-47, respectively. While Democrats are widely expected to reclaim the House, the Senate race remains closely contested, with the scale of any gains likely to determine how much of President Donald Trump’s agenda Republicans can advance during the final two years of his term.A Democratic victory in either chamber could pave the way for investigations into the Trump administration’s ethics, immigration enforcement and handling of the Iran war.Conversely, a strong Republican showing could reinforce Trump’s grip on the party, while heavy losses may intensify pressure to reconsider unpopular policies.Problems at polling stations and during the countElection officials have warned that close contests could lead to disputes over voter eligibility, ballot counting and certification. Long queues, machine malfunctions and challenges by partisan poll watchers could also fuel litigation and delay results.The Justice Department plans to deploy about 1,000 election monitors nationwide, roughly three times the number sent during the previous midterms. Some local officials fear their presence could intimidate voters, although the department has dismissed those concerns.Officials and legal experts are also watching for federal investigations or legal challenges that could disrupt certification.Several states are also unlikely to have complete results on election night, particularly in close races, potentially creating further disputes.How Trump responds to the resultsTrump’s reaction, particularly if Republicans lose control of Congress, could become a major story after polls close.In 2020, he declared victory before counting was complete and called for the process to stop. After losing to Joe Biden, he continued to falsely claim the election had been stolen, helping fuel the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol by supporters seeking to block certification of Biden’s victory.Trump’s administration has also sought voter data from states and launched investigations into suspected noncitizen voting, despite limited evidence of the practice. The Justice Department recently sued California over alleged noncitizen ballots.Voter turnoutTurnout among each party’s core supporters could prove decisive. Opinion polls showed Democrats were considerably more enthusiastic about voting than Republicans heading into Election Day.However, young, Black and Hispanic voters have historically participated at lower rates in midterms than in presidential elections. Surveys also indicate persistent scepticism towards both parties among these groups, particularly over the cost of living.If their turnout falls short of expectations, Democrats could underperform.What the results mean for 2028The midterms could influence the debate over who leads both parties into the next presidential election.Democrats remain divided between those advocating a more populist economic message and those favouring a centrist approach to win back swing voters. Strong performances by candidates from either camp could strengthen their respective arguments and shape the contest for the party’s 2028 nomination.The results could also offer an early indication of how voters view Trump’s policies and the direction of the Republican Party as it looks towards the next presidential race.You use AI every day. articles.title: Grain under fire: Russian, Ukrainian Black Sea attacks threaten food supply
articles.summary: Renewed strikes on Black Sea shipping imperil grain exports, drive up food prices and deepen global food insecurity.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – Three black naval drones resembling oversized plastic toys struck a freighter sluggishly navigating the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria on October 28.

Aerial drones joined the attack, and explosions rocked the Liberian-flagged Contship Jet Monrovia, loaded with more than 400 terracotta-coloured containers. The vessel, travelling from the Israeli port of Haifa to Romania, listed and sank, but all 18 crew members were rescued, Bulgarian authorities said.

The daytime assault was filmed by crew members, other ships and photographed by a French surveillance plane.

The drones were Russian, Kyiv claimed, adding that the attack was designed to make the Black Sea unsafe for civilian ships, paralyse Ukraine’s exports of grain and further hobble its war-ravaged economy.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv’s forces conducted “no operations in this part of the sea, and this latest tragedy involving civilian vessels is another part of Russia’s effort to make the western Black Sea completely unfit for navigation.”

The European Union’s delegation to Kyiv said in August that Russia is “systematically strangling Ukraine’s ability to feed the world.”

It added that by targeting ports, shipping lanes, and agricultural infrastructure, Moscow is not just waging war on Ukraine, but also “weaponising hunger against millions in Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.”

And while Europe’s food security is not at stake, the EU is “fully committed to continue supporting Ukraine’s access to international markets,” Paula Ritter-Moschutz, a spokeswoman for Agriculture and Customs at the European Commission, told Al Jazeera.

“We are continuously assessing its implications for agriculture, global food security, and the economy,” she said. “We support the initiatives for a moratorium on Black Sea attacks.”

At least 30 sailors have been killed or gone missing in the recent surge of attacks, according to Bulgarian and Romanian authorities and maritime tracking services.

“That makes business much more costly, not just dangerous,” Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey Analytics, a UK-based marine security consultancy .

Meanwhile, rising wheat prices “will put most pressure on the Global South when we inevitably see more disruption in the food supply,” he said. “And this will inevitably cause things like increased migration pressures in Northern Africa, and crossings across maritime domain of the Mediterranean as well as perhaps off the coast of the Canary Islands.”

Moscow’s alleged campaign follows Ukrainian strikes on Russian freighters and oil tankers in the Black Sea and the adjoining Sea of Azov amid attacks on oil refineries, military plants and warehouses.

Those strikes intensified in July, and Moscow’s suspected retaliatory attacks may have been prevented, observers say.

“A shadow deal [not to strike each other’s cargo ships] was breached by Ukraine in the summer,” Nikolay Mitrokhin, a researcher with Germany’s Bremen University who analyses the Russia-Ukraine war, told Al Jazeera.

Russian President Vladimir Putin “definitely liked the idea of completely ruining Ukrainian exports,” he said. “Putin did issue several warnings before systemic strikes on the Odesa group of ports began.”

“If the attacks on [Russian] tankers continue, we will consider taking retaliatory measures against ships from countries assisting Ukraine,” Putin said in December.

Russian farmers and grain exporters usually ship more than two-thirds of their harvests via the Black Sea. As a result of the lack of security, they are testing exporting grain through the Arctic port of Murmansk, though the distance between the farms and the buyers will significantly increase costs.

Before Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, about a third of the world’s grain exports passed through the Black Sea, and Ukraine provided a tenth of global wheat exports and 15 percent of corn.

Ukraine’s customers include Middle East and North African nations.

Over the past 12 months, wheat prices rose by a fifth.

Chicago wheat futures, a global benchmark for the wheat market, have gone up from $5.03 per bushel (35 litres) in October 2025 to $6.03 in October this year.

The US-Israel war on Iran, global warming and a drought in South Africa have also contributed to the spike.

Constant Russian strikes by jet-powered drones, cruise and ballistic missiles brought operations in Ukraine’s largest maritime hub, Odesa, to a halt.

“Today, after the ports of Odesa are paralysed, there’s no way out. Hardly more than 50 percent of grain can be exported via land routes,” Viktor Honcharenko, president of the Association of Farmers and Private Land Owners of Ukraine, told Al Jazeera. “Lots of wheat remained on the fields, it’s not being harvested,” he said.

The consequences will have a domino effect on Ukraine’s entire economy.

“There will be penniless farmers, penniless medium-sized businesses, taxes will practically be not paid, the state budget won’t get any money, and jobs will be lost,” Honcharenko said.

The paralysis of maritime grain shipments will mostly affect small farmers because larger, industrial farms will be first to export their grains via railroads and on trucks, he said.

Up to 60 million tonnes of grain have been harvested in Ukraine this year, but only half can be shipped out of the country, according to Kyiv-based analyst Aleksey Kushch.

Ukraine’s overloaded railroads cannot get larger volumes out of the country, he said.

To make use of its grain surplus, Ukraine could develop domestic production of flour, starches, glues and paper-making additives. However the country had lost its opportunity to “start full-scale processing”, Kushch told Al Jazeera.

Ukraine could switch to producing legumes and oil crops that would be welcome in the EU, whose member states defend domestic wheat farmers, but are interested in producing vegetable oils and protein.

But that would significantly decrease Ukrainian farmers’ profits, and that is where Zelenskyy’s government should have stepped in to negotiate EU subsidies for growing chickpeas and soy, Kushch said.

“The price of the matter is one billion euros,” he added, referring to the estimated cost of subsidies.

articles.title: How Florida Governor Ron DeSantis will shape his state’s 2026 midterm race
articles.summary: The outgoing governor and former presidential candidate has transformed Florida into a conservative policy vanguard.
articles.body:
Few modern governors have left as deep a mark on Florida’s character as Republican Ron DeSantis.

Across his two terms, the 48-year-old politician has overhauled the state’s political landscape, turning what was once a swing state into a Republican stronghold.

The Florida governor has also established himself as a key national figure in United States politics. During the 2024 presidential race, he was considered one of the chief Republican challengers to President Donald Trump.

DeSantis leaves office in January: Due to term limits, he cannot run in a third election for governor.

But experts say his legacy as a hardline Republican will define the race to succeed him in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

US Representative Byron Donalds is campaigning to defend the Republicans’ hold on the governor’s mansion in Florida, but he faces stiffer-than-expected competition from former Congress member David Jolly, a centrist Democrat.

“Was [DeSantis’s position] going to alienate some voters? It definitely has. We’ll find out tomorrow if it’s enough to make a change,” Aubrey Jewett, a political science professor at the University of Central Florida, told Al Jazeera.

A decade ago, DeSantis was hardly the household name he is today in the US.

A former naval officer who served three terms in the US House of Representatives, the Republican was by no means a shoo-in for the governor’s chair when he first ran for office in 2018.

The race was tight. Even with Trump’s endorsement, DeSantis only scraped past his Democratic rival, Andrew Gillum, by less than half a percentage point.

At the time, Florida was a quintessential “purple” state, capable of leaning towards either Republican or Democrat.

Under DeSantis’s leadership, however, the state took a rightward turn. The last Democrat to win statewide office in Florida was Nikki Fried, the former agricultural commissioner – and her victory came eight years ago.

Ever since, Democrats in Florida have endured a dry spell, while the Republican margin of victory has grown.

In 2022, for instance, DeSantis overwhelmingly won re-election by 19 points, the largest gap since 1982. He also became the first Republican gubernatorial candidate in 20 years to win the Democratic stronghold of Miami-Dade County.

By Trump’s re-election in 2024, Florida’s reputation as a reliably red bastion was undeniable.

Trump notched a decisive victory with 13.1 percentage points over former Vice President Kamala Harris in Florida’s presidential vote that year, a far cry from his wafer-thin 1.2-point advantage during the 2016 election.

According to Florida’s Division of Elections, Republicans currently hold an advantage of 1.5 million registered voters over the state’s Democrats.

That is a dramatic reversal from 2020, when Democrats held a registration advantage of at least 100,000 voters.

Many experts credit DeSantis with spearheading this registration surge. Republicans have been attracted to the state by DeSantis’s platform of low taxes and light regulations, as well as his rejection of pandemic-era restrictions.

Trump himself made the Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Florida, his permanent residence in 2019, in a move widely speculated to take advantage of Florida’s favourable tax regime.

Though Trump and DeSantis were briefly rivals during the 2024 Republican primaries, Jewett said the Florida governor has helped shape the meaning of “Trumpism”, the president’s political movement.

DeSantis himself has held up Florida as a “blueprint for America’s revival”.

Under his leadership, Florida has participated in Trump’s immigration crackdown and sought to purge public universities of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives.

In April 2022, for instance, he signed into law the Stop Woke Act, which limited how race and gender were taught in public schools by barring instruction that portrayed any group as “inherently racist”.

Part of the law was later struck down after advocates argued that it constituted censorship in violation of the First Amendment of the Constitution.

Other DeSantis-era laws, like 2022’s Parental Rights in Education Act, curbed classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity.

“Those things have been cemented in Florida’s K-12 system,” Jewett explained. “There’s not a lot that the school boards could do, given that the governor has removed several people for policy disagreements.”

Those laws, however, had wide-reaching impact across the US.

States like Arkansas, Indiana, Kentucky and Iowa subsequently pursued laws curtailing how public schools addressed sexuality, gender identity and race in the classroom.

As Floridians head to the polls to choose DeSantis’s successor, Jewett said DeSantis will cast a long shadow over state and national politics for years to come.

“Whether anyone agrees or disagrees with [DeSantis], from a neutral political science perspective, the man has had a huge impact in Florida and across the nation,” he said.

Donalds, the Republican, has pledged to continue DeSantis-style politics, calling the outgoing leader “best governor in the country”. While in the US Congress, Donalds even sponsored legislation to limit how gender and race are taught, echoing DeSantis’s own legislative platform.

His challenger Jolly, a Republican-turned-Democrat, is pitching himself as an alternative to “partisan politics”, with affordability and healthcare at the heart of his campaign.

Jewett expects Donalds to preserve much of DeSantis’s right-wing agenda, though not necessarily replicate his approach to all subjects, including Black history.

The DeSantis administration has previously been accused of attempting to sanitise the teaching of slavery by rejecting an Advanced Placement course on African American history.

“Maybe on the racial issue […], you might see a little bit of softening there,” Jewett said of Donalds.

He cautioned, however, that Donalds was likely “not going to turn into a progressive on those issues either”.

DeSantis, meanwhile, is unlikely to disappear from national politics.

“I don’t think we’ve seen the last of him,” Jewett said. He predicts DeSantis will “certainly try to run for president again” in 2028.

articles.title: '24 hours have passed, Modi ji': Rahul renews debate challenge to PM over 'foreign links' - watch
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Turning his Diwali greetings into another political jab with “a red rose”, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday renewed
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Turning his Diwali greetings into another political jab with “a red rose”, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday renewed his challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi to face him in an open debate, saying 24 hours had passed since he dared the PM.In a video shared on X, Rahul said, “24 hours have passed, Modi ji. I challenged you. You say that the opposition is anti-national. Pick any stage, any venue, and debate me.”“Who is the anti-national? Who has connections with foreign forces? And what kind of connections are they? Do it as soon as possible, don't be afraid,” he said.The Congress leader's remarks came 24 hours after he challenged the Prime Minister to an open debate on the allegations of him of becoming Prime Minister with "foreign help" saying the latter would not dare to accept it.In the video, Rahul proposed that the debate be held in the presence of the media and the country's youth, with both leaders seated across a table.He also said PM Modi could choose the person who would moderate or judge the discussion, suggesting RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat for the role.“We'll both be there, the media will be there, the youth of the country will be there, there'll be a table, you'll sit on one side, I'll sit on the other. Whoever you want to appoint as judge, go ahead. Put Mohan Bhagwat ji in the chair, come on. And then we'll debate,” he said.Listing the issues he wanted to discuss, Rahul referred to the financial system, the “US deal, the Adani case and Jeffrey Epstein.”“Questions will come up about the financial system, the financial structure, how the US deal happened, why it happened, why so quickly, why you did it alone, why you didn't tell the Cabinet, why the Adani case was closed, Epstein—there are so many things like that on which we'll have an open discussion,” he said.“Come on, don't be afraid. (Doodh ka doodh pani ka pani kijiye) Separate the milk from the water,” he added.Rahul also referred to the defamation cases filed against him over other issues and challenged the Prime Minister to take legal action over his allegations of foreign connections.“You make allegations against me, don't you? Come on, everything will be cleared up. On other matters, you've slapped me with defamation cases—maybe 45 defamation cases against me,” he said.“But on this debate issue, on foreign connections, you're not filing defamation. Go ahead, file one—we'll discuss that openly too,” he added.Rahul ended the video by repeating his call for an early debate, saying, “Let’s do this as soon as possible. Daro mat!” He signed off with a Diwali greeting to the Prime Minister: “Happy Diwali, Modi ji.”His fresh challenge came hours after Union minister Kiren Rijiju criticised him over his allegation that PM Modi became Prime Minister with “foreign help”.Taking a swipe at Rahul, Rijiju compared his remarks to Islamic fundamentalists speaking about secularism, separatists carrying Indian flags and anarchists displaying the Constitution.In a post on X, the minister said, “It's the same as islamic fundamentalists talking about secularism, separatists holding Indian flags & anarchists showing Constitution book. articles.title: Scotland needs to embrace AI for its potential to be realised, minister says
articles.summary: The Scottish government has said AI could generate an additional £23bn in annual GDP for Scotland by 2035 with the right investment and leadership.
articles.body:
Scotland needs to embrace AI technology and trust the country's planning system to allow its potential to be realised, Innovation Minister Alyn Smith has said.

The Scottish government said AI could generate an additional £23bn in annual GDP for Scotland by 2035 with the right investment and leadership, citing independent research .

It comes at a time of widespread debate about the technology's value, as well as opposition to a number of proposed AI data centres in Scotland.

Smith told the BBC: "People are up for these developments but we need to see the planning system augmented to take due note of the significant implications of some of these projects, particularly on energy use."

The minister is due to attend a meeting in Edinburgh to hear from businesses about what they feel is holding back AI adoption and what is helping.

The event will also discuss the role of Scotland's universities and colleges in developing the AI and data skills the economy needs.

In September, the Scottish Greens led a debate calling for a pause on planning applications for large-scale AI data centres until national guidance had been published.

The Scottish government officially rejected this, though ministers said consent for such sites was "highly unlikely" to be granted before guidance is updated by the end of this year.

The government said that while there were "legitimate concerns" about large data centres, ministers were increasing oversight of the planning process.

Smith said some of the arguments surrounding the building of large data centres had been leading the conversation about the future of AI in Scotland.

"Some of the discourse we have seen on this is wild," Smith told Radio Scotland Breakfast .

"You'd think there wasn't a planning system at all. Comparing a really bad data centre in the middle of the Utah desert doesn't track through to what we're going to have in Scotland."

BBC Scotland has previously heard from people living near proposed data centre sites who worry about the appearance of developments, potential noise and the amount of land required to build them.

Experts have also warned MSPs that these data centres could push up electricity prices for consumers and challenge climate change targets.

Meanwhile the Scottish Greens say an unregulated expansion of data centres would "enrich giant AI companies and their super-rich owners".

Smith said the Scottish people were "pro-technology", pointing out that the IT industry in Scotland currently employs 87,000 people compared with the 21,000 people employed by the mining industry in 1979.

"Lets just get a grip on this," he said. "The people of Scotland are serious about technological developments. We've got a great industry right now."

He said there needed to be "confidence-building measures" in AI going forward.

"I want to see us get a grip on this debate - focus on the actual facts," he said. "We could get significant community benefit out of these things."

Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing

How could AI change Scotland's public services?

Smith said data centres were "the whisky bonds of the AI sector".

"They're an integral part of what the sector needs to be and for tech sovereignty in a really interconnected, but unstable world, I think it's quite important that if you're using a smartphone you ask where your data is being kept. Is it somewhere reliable? Is it somewhere trustworthy?"

Smith admitted that there were not a great deal of jobs created by data centres but emphasised the benefits AI could bring to businesses and the community.

Speaking about the concerns raised over data centres, he said: "Everything will be judged on its merit. People who are expressing concerns about particular developments, so they should. We have a planning system in Scotland that the people are in charge of.

"Not all of these applications are going to go forward because not all of them are suitable or have sufficient community engagement.

"We are a tech-heavy nation. We have got a lot of great jobs in this sector and I want a debate on the merit of these AI data centres."

The minister said a new Workplace Jobs Observatory - led by STUC - could examine in real time how AI was impacting on the workplace.

"This is a technology that is developing at pace," he said. "I want to see ethical guard rails put on it by legislation and want to align with the EU norms."

He said Tuesday's meeting would look at what the Scottish government was doing to adopt the technology and to make sure people had the relevant skills.

"Where there are opportunities for AI I want us to be all over it," he said. "And where there are things that people need to be reassured about I also want to be all over it because I'm here to represent the interests of the people of Scotland."

Julian David, chief executive of techUK, who is also attending the meeting, said: "The opportunity AI offers Scotland is significant, but it will only be realised if businesses and government pull in the same direction.

"Today's roundtable is a chance for industry to share what is working on the ground and for government to listen and act.

"By collaborating, we can help more businesses of every size make the most of AI."

articles.title: Norfolk data centre and solar plan sees hundreds attend meeting
articles.summary: People spilled out of the hall in Norfolk, trying to follow proceedings.
articles.body:
More than 400 people were at a public meeting to share concerns about plans to build what would be one of the UK's biggest data centres and accompanying solar farms.

The Longmarsh Green Energy (LGE) project would cover 4,695 acres (1,900 hectares) of farmland across two sites south of King's Lynn in Norfolk.

Dr Martin Little, who leads the Stop Longmarsh Energy (SLE) campaign group, said the proposal would "destroy" farming land.

LGE, which revealed the plans last month, said they "welcome comments during this consultation period".

The hall at Tilney St Lawrence was full on Monday evening, with locals even following proceedings from the car park.

Farmer James Kitchen grows wheat, barley and oilseed rape on land that would neighbour the data centre.

He said he was "gobsmacked" to hear about the project.

Natural England, a public body which advises the government, classifies the affected area as grade one - meaning it is "excellent quality agricultural land".

"We've got some really good heavy silt land here - it's very good at producing good quality produce," said Kitchen.

Despite this year's drought, he said his yields were still high because of the way the soil in the Fens retains moisture.

Resident Amanda Naish said the project would ruin the countryside views she currently enjoyed.

"I just feel like I'm living in a nightmare," she said.

"I'm not against AI. I think it's a necessity for us all going forward. I just think that there needs to be thought, there needs to be balance."

David Rutter, who lives in the village, has been researching data centres since receiving a letter from LGE explaining the plans.

He fears the noise will be heard up to a mile away and will effect human health and the environment including birds.

Little, who lives in the village, said he was proud to be a so-called nimby - an acronym for "not in my back yard".

"Everybody - and I do mean everybody - is a nimby when the time comes.

"If anyone out there thinks they aren't a nimby, come and buy my house from me and live surrounded by glass for the rest of time."

Little echoed the views of those who spoke at the meeting, saying they were not against data centres or solar farms, but that they should be smaller in scale and on brownfield sites.

Referring to the potential loss of farmland, he added: "Is it dinner or data? It's as simple as that."

How has community reacted to major data centre plan?

LGE was invited to the meeting - which was organised by the local parish council - but declined.

In a statement, it said: "We have already received helpful feedback during the community consultation.

"We are committed to working with residents nearest to the proposals to develop site-specific mitigation measures, including appropriate planting, screening and landscape treatments prior to submission."

South West Norfolk MP Terry Jermy said the meeting turnout had been "amazing".

"Food security is absolutely crucial," he said. "We cannot have improving energy security but worsening food security."

The Labour politician said he would be pushing for a ban on solar farms being built on farmland which is classed as grade two or higher.

Parts of Europe already have restrictions on placing solar farms on high quality farming land, including across Italy and in parts of Spain.

In last week's Budget, the chancellor announced a Data Centre Covenant, requiring operators to invest in local communities , create jobs and protect water supplies in return for the best grid connections.

The scale of the proposal deems it a nationally significant infrastructure project, so the ultimate decision rests with the government rather than the local council.

A public consultation is open via the project's website until 26 November. An application is due to be submitted by April 2027.

It could take six months for the plans to be examined by the Planning Inspectorate. A decision could be made by July 2028.

articles.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy on defying US in attacking Russian oil: 'Our response must be painful'
articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News Ukraine will keep striking Russian oil refineries unless Trump delivers Patriot missiles to shield energy infrastructure.
articles.body: KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is defying calls from the Trump administration for his armed forces to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, telling Fox News: "Our response must be painful." In an interview in Kyiv, Zelenskyy acknowledged holding discussions with the Trump administration about targeting oil facilities, attacks President Donald Trump has pinned as being partly to blame for high gas prices in the U.S. "We had different conversations — different, and several — with President Trump and with his team about attacks on refineries," Zelenskyy said. "We said that if you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system." TRUMP TELLS ZELENSKYY TO STOP DOING 'ONE THING' DURING ATTACKS ON RUSSIA Ukraine has reported near-daily Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, triggering power outages just as temperatures dip ahead of winter. "That's why we have to respond. But our response has to be painful for Russian military people," Zelenskyy said. "If we will not respond on energy, they will continue." U.S.-Ukraine relations took a further hit in October when Trump struck a deal to import millions of tons of Russian diesel to the United States. ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE Zelenskyy suggested Ukraine might be encouraged to hold off on further attacks on Russian oil facilities if the United States were to deliver more U.S.-made Patriot missile interceptors to protect Ukrainian skies. Pressed by Fox News on whether that might be seen as an attempt to leverage Trump, Zelenskyy said: "I don't have any concerns when I share the truth between partners." "Our countries are huge partners. American society (is a) huge supporter." "And that's why I have to share with (the) president the truth, the real situation: that America can't help Russia. (The) president can't help Putin." US WILL MEDIATE UPCOMING UKRAINE-RUSSIA TALKS IN ABU DHABI, WITKOFF SAYS Ahead of planned peace talks in the United Arab Emirates, Zelenskyy urged Trump to launch another push for a targeted ceasefire where both Russia and Ukraine refrain from attacks on energy facilities. "If the American president thinks that this war has influence on the prices," Zelenskyy said, "he can ask, energy ceasefire, during (the) Abu Dhabi trilateral meeting: energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy spoke with Fox News hours before starved and exhausted residents left the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky and crossed into Ukraine under a humanitarian truce brokered by first lady Melania Trump, the first of its kind in more than four years of war. articles.title: Hampshire Reform UK councillor charged with rape and sexual assault
articles.summary: The Crown Prosecution Service has charged George Madgwick with 35 offences, including 12 counts of rape.
articles.body:
The leader of Reform UK in Hampshire has been charged with 35 offences against four victims over a 13-year period, including 12 counts of rape.

The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said it had charged George Madgwick with the offences, which it said took place between 2008 and 2021 in Portsmouth and Wales.

It said the 37-year-old faced charges including rape, sexual assault, controlling or coercive behaviour, and making indecent images of a child against four victims - who were aged 16 and 17 at the time.

Reform UK said Madgwick had been suspended "with immediate effect". He is due to appear at Portsmouth Magistrates' Court on 25 November.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said its investigation into Madgwick began on 24 July 2025, after receiving a report of a sexual offence.

The force said it first arrested him on 6 January 2026, before he was charged by the CPS on Tuesday.

In total, Madgwick, who is from the the Anchorage Park area of Portsmouth, has been charged with 12 counts of rape, two counts of assault by penetration and two of sexual assault.

Madgwick has also been charged with two counts of making indecent images of children, two of controlling or coercive behaviour and eight of assault occasioning actual bodily harm.

He faces one charge each of causing or inciting sexual exploitation of a child, distributing an indecent image of a child, stalking, making threats to kill, false imprisonment, theft and criminal damage.

A spokesperson for the CPS said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence and that it is in the public interest to bring the case to court.

"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are now active and that he has the right to a fair trial. There should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in any way prejudice these proceedings."

The 37-year-old councillor represents North East Havant on Hampshire County Council and Paulsgrove on Portsmouth City Council.

Madgwick was elected to his position on the county council by a large margin in May - just months after he was first arrested by police.

Last month, he featured in the the ITV News Exposure documentary Undercover: A Year In Reform - after which he accused the broadcaster of "electoral interference".

In the programme, he was shown voicing support for the Portsmouth Patriots anti-immigration group.

He subsequently issued a statement saying the undercover reporters potentially had an "impact on the result" of council elections.

articles.title: From Italy to Canada, how the UK’s Palestine Action group went global
articles.summary: The banned UK group, which targets Israel’s war machine, has inspired activists in Europe and beyond.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – In November 2023, protesters spray painted the Rome headquarters of Leonardo, an Italian weapons manufacturer with ongoing contracts with Israel.

The group was inspired by a Palestine Action protest against Leonardo’s Edinburgh factory that same month, which resulted in the factory being shut down.

“That was the first movement, where, in Italy, we felt we needed to do something,” said Luca, a representative from the group, simply named Palestine Action Italy.

It is one of several global offshoots of the proscribed UK group, Palestine Action.

Other groups sharing the Palestine Action name exist elsewhere, including in the Netherlands, Ireland, Spain, France and Canada.

Last week, a subsidiary of Elbit, Israel’s largest weapons maker and the target of Palestine Action’s campaign, in Canada was raided and spray-painted by a group of activists operating under Palestine Action Canada.

Beyond those protesting under the same name, other organisations have also adopted Palestine Action’s direct action tactics of physically targeting arms manufacturers supplying Israel and other companies alleged to be complicit in the genocide of Palestinians, rather than pursuing indirect forms of pressure such as voting, lobbying or legal negotiation.

As Al Jazeera has reported, similar protest groups have organised in the Czech Republic and Germany.

Stop Arming Israel France is dedicated to action against French arms producers, while Global Sumud Flotilla Italy works to intercept cargo ships carrying arms-related materials into Italian ports.

“The direct action movement is growing across the world,” Huda Ammori, cofounder of Palestine Action, told Al Jazeera. “In order for the Israeli weapons industry to operate, it requires a global supply chain and a presence in countries across the world. Those sites are pressure points which ordinary people can disrupt to bring down the Israeli war machine.”

Palestine Action Italy began as a small movement mirroring the British group, but has amassed tens of thousands of social media followers and staged several occupations of Leonardo’s facilities.

They work with other Palestine Action groups in Europe to host training sessions on direct action, teaching others how to occupy and disrupt the work of weapons producers across the continent.

“Palestine Action is the closest way to be against the war. They are creating weapons, we are destroying them,” said Luca, a representative of the Italian group.

In Italy’s waters, activists also take cues.

Last month, local activists and others associated with the Global Sumud Flotilla Italia (GSF Italy) group used three small ships to intercept the Sundaid X, a container ship with military cargo.

The group said the cargo directly supplied nearby Sigonella naval air base and drone hub, “serving as a primary logistics pipeline for US military operations and ongoing conflicts across West Asia”.

Police detained the activists, accusing them of disrupting public order.

M, a spokesperson for Global Sumud Flotilla Italia, cited the direct action tactics of climate justice movements like Extinction Rebellion and the work of Palestine Action as important influences in Italy’s pro-Palestine direct action organising.

When asked about Palestine Action, M said, “[Italian activists] know them very well.”

According to her, arrests are a sign the group’s efforts are working.

In France last week, more than 20 activists blocked access to the headquarters of Safran Data Systems in Les Ulis, forcing the company to evacuate several employees and disrupting almost three hours of work.

Safran Data Systems is part of Safran Electronics and Defense, a French company with ties to Israel’s military. This includes producing fighter jet parts and a partnership with Israeli arms manufacturer Rafael dating back to 2021, where the two companies have worked to develop sensor technology that “reduced the time of the average time to close a [kill chain] to less than half a second,” a Rafael representative said in 2022.

Stop Arming Israel France, which was among the organisers, focuses on protests and direct action against companies producing military equipment for Israel and trade fairs showcasing them.

“The aim is to disrupt the business-as-usual activities of the ‘merchants of death’ and have a tangible impact on the trade taking place at these fairs,” Stop Arming Israel France’s spokesperson, who wished to remain anonymous, said.

“The actions carried out by Palestine Action are a source of inspiration for many activists in France and encourage them to take action themselves,” the spokesperson said.

Still, they underlined their support for both direct action and other forms of protest, for those not comfortable with the possible risks associated with direct action, such as being sentenced as “terrorists”.

Occupation is a commonly mirrored tactic that often carries less risk than property damage or vandalism, but can still disrupt the flow of goods and services for prolonged periods.

In Canada, charges were recently dropped against activists who occupied a Montreal branch of Scotiabank to protest against investments in Elbit Systems. The protesters were removed by police in riot gear in the 2024 action. In February, Scotiabank divested from Elbit Systems.

In July 2025, Palestine Action was proscribed as a “terrorist organisation” in the UK.

“Their repression demonstrates to ordinary people how effective direct action is. It is precisely because direct action threatens the Israeli war machine, that they must [throw] everything at our movement to protect the military-industrial complex,” said Ammori.

Since the proscription, at least 4,000 people have been arrested for charges related to the group.

This includes the thousands of largely peaceful protestors who have been arrested for holding signs reading, “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action” at demonstrations regularly organised by protest group Defend Our Juries.

On Wednesday, the UK-based group heads to court again to fight the ban.

“Our democracies have failed us; that’s why direct action is important,” said Luca of Palestine Action Italy.

In August 2026, the United States sanctioned Palestine Action alongside several other pro-Palestine organisations. As a result, Palestine Action Italy lost access to their donation platform, which was US-based.

“We’re pretty sure that as soon as they realise how powerful [Palestine Action Italy] is in Italy, they will follow the UK’s footsteps,” said Luca of Palestine Action Italy. “We are getting ready to face this level of sacrifice: when we have to switch from being considered activists to being considered terrorists.”

articles.summary: VARANASI: \"I become CM when I don't contest elections,\" Samajwadi Party (SP) chief Akhilesh Yadav said on Tuesday, indicating that he would not contest
articles.body: VARANASI: "I become CM when I don't contest elections," Samajwadi Party (SP) chief Akhilesh Yadav said on Tuesday, indicating that he would not contest the upcoming UP assembly elections.Speaking to the media, SP supermo said, "I become CM when don't contest elections. In past I had gone to swear in as CM while being a Lok Sabha member"."This time also I will go to swear in as CM from Lok Sabha," he said, replying to a question on whether he would try his luck from any assembly seat in Varanasi.On a lighter note, Yadav said people in Kashi (Varanasi) consider auspicious timings before filing their nomination papers. He added that he would also do what he considered auspicious for himself.Earlier, Akhilesh Yadav had attacked the BJP following the Uttar Pradesh MLC election results, saying the party's "double-engine" government had been reduced to "double zero" in key constituencies.The BJP won six of the 11 seats, while the SP secured five. The biggest setback for the BJP came in Varanasi, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's parliamentary constituency, where the SP won both the Teachers' and Graduates' seats.Akhilesh said the results reflected growing anger among teachers, students and educated unemployed graduates ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections.Yadav became the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh in March 2012, at the age of 38, after the Samajwadi Party won 224 of the 403 Assembly seats, securing an absolute majority. He had not contested the Assembly election that year and entered the state legislature through the Legislative Council. He took oath as chief minister on March 15, 2012.He served as chief minister until 2017, when the SP lost power to the BJP. The party's tally fell from 224 seats in 2012 to 47 in 2017. articles.title: Bodycam video shows aftermath of fatal shooting by National Guard in Memphis
articles.summary: Tennessee National Guard troops in Memphis last summer trained their handguns on Tyrin Johnson as he lay dying on a sidewalk after a guard member shot him in the back, video released Monday by county prosecutors shows.
articles.body: NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Tennessee National Guard troops in Memphis last summer trained their handguns on a man as he lay dying on a sidewalk after a guard member shot him in the back, video released Monday by county prosecutors shows. A Memphis police officer can be heard in the footage from an officer’s body camera calling for an ambulance and then asking the troops, “Hey, you guys got a medical kit or anything?” The Shelby County District Attorney’s Office released the videos, which also include footage from stationary cameras and a cellphone from a bystander, as the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation continues its investigation into the July 5 shooting of Tyrin Johnson. Johnson, 20, who had been armed, died at the scene from a single gunshot wound, according to investigators. An autopsy report shared by Johnson’s family found that he was shot in the back, contradicting police and National Guard accounts that said he was facing the guard members with a gun when they fired at him. The footage did not show Johnson’s initial encounter with the guard members or them firing at him. The guard members were part of a federal task force created by President Donald Trump, who last year sent troops and federal agents to Democrat-run cities that he described as overrun with crime. Tennessee’s Republican Gov. Bill Lee had deployed the Guard to support the effort. The task force was involved in four fatal shootings between May and July. District Attorney Steve Mulroy said he has not yet decided whether to file charges in connection with the death. A spokesperson for the Tennessee National Guard did not immediately respond to email and phone messages seeking comment. Ed Yarbrough, an attorney for the two guard members, said they have no comment at this time. Authorities said the troops were responding with local police to reports of gunshots around 4 a.m. when they began pursuing an armed man fleeing on foot. Footage from stationary street cameras shows a person in dark clothing firing shots through an empty parking lot at three people walking on a sidewalk. Two Memphis police officers hear gunshots nearby and start walking and then running in that direction, a body camera worn by one of the officers shows. The officers say on their radio that they are pursuing a man who is running and armed with a gun. The video, which is blurry from the officer’s movement, captures yelling and the sound of a single gunshot, followed by several additional gunshot noises. A Tennessee National Guard report obtained by The Associated Press via a public records request said two guard members responded to the Memphis police radio call, left their vehicle and approached the suspect, who “rounded on them and pointed a tan handgun at them.” Both guard members fired their service weapons — M17 handguns — and Memphis police arrived shortly after, the report stated. Police body camera footage shows guard members at the scene shouting “Hands!” and “Turn over!” as they point their handguns at a man lying on his back on the sidewalk. André C. Wharton, an attorney for Johnson’s family, noted that the videos do not show the moments immediately before the shooting, or the shooting itself. “This investigation must stay focused on the moment the guardsman fired the fatal shot and whether that action was reasonable,” Wharton said. Johnson was the father of a young child and was preparing to help lead the family construction business, his grandfather, Evaniel Johnson, said. At least six guard members were on the scene immediately after the shooting, the body camera video shows. One can be seen moving a handgun that is on the ground until a police officer tells him to leave it alone. An officer calls for an ambulance over the radio, and a guard member begins to cut off the man’s shirt just before the video ends.
