articles.title: Nike faces religious ban in Libya because it was named after Greek goddess
articles.summary: The US company was named after the Greek goddess of victory, so the Dar al-Ifta said displaying its logo was unIslamic.
articles.body:
Libya's highest religious authority, the Dar al-Ifta, has issued a ruling banning Muslims from buying, selling or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo.

The ruling, issued by the Tripoli-based institution, states that the US sportswear giant was named after the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo was inspired by her wings.

It argued that wearing clothing displaying the logo amounted to promoting symbols associated "with polytheism," or the worship of more than one god.

Libya is home to the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, where archaeological remains include a statue of the Greek goddess of the same name.

The religious committee also accused Nike of supporting Israel and called for a boycott of companies that back the country.

It referred to a statement issued by its Council for Research and Sharia Studies on 5 November 2023, urging Muslims to boycott Western companies it considers supportive of Israel during the war in Gaza.

The ruling, known as a fatwa, is a religious opinion on a matter of Islamic law. It was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani.

The Dar al-Ifta is an influential religious institution based in Tripoli, in western Libya. The country is politically divided, with rival authorities and institutions operating in the east and west after years of conflict following the toppling of long-time leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

Although its religious rulings can carry considerable social influence, they are not necessarily government orders or legally enforceable.

Last year it ruled against wearing jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels, arguing that its four-leaf clover design was associated with Christian beliefs and the pursuit of good luck, which it said contradicted Islamic teachings.

The latest fatwa does not announce a state ban on Nike products or specify penalties for people who continue to buy or wear them.

Social media reactions were mixed, with some users welcoming the ruling, while others questioned its significance, describing it as ironic or a distraction from more pressing issues.

The ruling comes amid wider debates over the rise of religious conservatism in public life in Libya.

In 2025, authorities in eastern Libya announced restrictions on rap music, theatre and dance performances, citing concerns that some lyrics and performances violated public morals and Islamic values.

The measures were subsequently extended to western Libya.

The Dar al-Ifta has also previously issued religious rulings against music, although there is no clear evidence that it was directly involved in the restrictions on performances.

Nike does not operate an official store in Libya, however Nike-branded products are available through local sportswear retailers.

Sportswear brands such as Nike and Adidas are popular across North Africa.

In Libya, as in other countries in the region, counterfeit versions of popular sportswear brands are also sold in local markets.

articles.title: Global food security is under threat
articles.summary: Attacks on grain shipments from Russia and Ukraine may drive up food prices, hitting import-dependent countries hardest.
articles.body:
Attacks on commercial vessels appear to have become an established tactic in ongoing wars. In the Gulf region, they are part of the continuing war of attrition between the United States and Iran. In the Black Sea, they have become an increasingly prominent feature of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. Most of the vessels being targeted are not military ships but commercial ones carrying oil, gas and petroleum products, or food commodities such as wheat and corn. All are essential either to the functioning of the economy or to human survival.

In October, commercial shipping in the Black Sea witnessed a sharp escalation, with a series of drone attacks targeting at least nine vessels off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, both NATO members. This is a dangerous development through which Moscow is testing the alliance’s cohesion. Several NATO members have already complained of Russian incursions into their territory, raising questions about whether Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, which provides for collective defence, could be invoked.

Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukrainian ports on the Black Sea and the Danube River. With most Ukrainian ports disrupted, Kyiv has turned to alternative routes to export its grain to markets in Africa and the Middle East. These fall into three main categories:

The Danube corridor through Romania: Grain is transported from Ukraine’s interior to the ports of Izmail and Reni on the Danube, then through Romania’s Sulina Channel to the Black Sea, or to the Romanian port of Constanta, where it is transferred to larger vessels.

Overland corridors through the European Union: Ukraine uses trains and trucks to transport grain through Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and Romania, from where it is shipped through European ports on the Baltic, Adriatic or Black Seas.

The Ukrainian maritime corridor along NATO coastlines: Departing from ports in the Odesa region, ships travel through the western Black Sea, close to the waters of Romania and Bulgaria, then towards Turkiye, before passing through the Bosphorus Strait to reach global markets.

But these alternative corridors have not escaped Russian attacks. According to a report by maritime security company Ambrey , the monthly rate of attacks associated with the Danube corridor was 3.7 times higher in the July-September quarter than in the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, the Danube’s share of cargo handled at Ukrainian ports jumped from about 10 percent during January-June to 74 percent in August 2026.

Seeking to inflict maximum damage and losses on each other, neither Russia nor Ukraine has shied away from using every available means to deter or subdue the other. While the war initially focused on military and logistical facilities, attacks subsequently expanded to infrastructure and ports, then gradually to refineries and energy installations. Today, food-related facilities and ships carrying grain and other food products are increasingly in the line of fire.

At the beginning of the war, Moscow concentrated its strikes on Ukraine’s infrastructure for producing grain and oilseeds. It obstructed access to Ukrainian ports on the Black Sea and repeatedly targeted vessels carrying grain. This forced Ukraine to secure alternative export routes, including the Danube, which has itself become a target of Russian attacks.

Grain and vegetable oil exports are a vital part of Ukraine’s economy. Data indicate that they accounted for about 40 percent of the country’s total merchandise exports in the first half of this year. This helps explain why Russia has concentrated its strikes on ports and vessels transporting these economically vital products.

Ukraine’s agriculture minister estimates that if the ports remain closed, the country will lose at least $8bn between June this year and June 2027. That shortfall would be equivalent to 20 percent of its total export revenues last year. Russian attacks on cargo vessels and export infrastructure have largely brought maritime traffic through Ukraine’s Black Sea ports to a halt. These ports previously handled about 90 percent of the country’s agricultural exports.

On the other side, Russian grain production and exports had, until recently, remained relatively insulated from attacks. But this summer, Kyiv redirected its drones towards Russian grain and vegetable oil export facilities, as well as commercial vessels, including grain carriers.

This marked a significant shift in the economic war, as Ukrainian strikes had previously focused more heavily on Russian energy installations and military facilities. Ukrainian attacks disrupted main Russian grain export terminals on the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, forcing Moscow to divert some of its exports to Baltic Sea ports. The Sea of Azov had previously handled nearly a quarter of Russia’s wheat exports.

Russia is the world’s largest wheat exporter, while Ukraine ranks fifth. Together, they account for nearly 27 percent of global wheat exports. Recent attacks have pushed wheat futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange to their highest levels since 2023, with prices rising by about 20 percent in the first nine months of this year.

The escalation of attacks by both sides has coincided with the peak wheat export season in each country. Winter wheat, the dominant variety grown in Russia and Ukraine, is harvested in summer and exported in late summer and early autumn.

Ukrainian attacks, particularly those targeting Russian ports on the Sea of Azov and at Novorossiysk, have reportedly knocked out an estimated 70 percent of Russia’s grain export capacity. Recent Russian attacks, meanwhile, have halted shipments from Odesa, putting nearly 90 percent of Ukrainian grain shipments out of operation.

Ukraine also intensified its attacks on cargo ships departing Russian ports in July and August. According to Ukrainian military officials, they struck 76 Russian vessels between July 6 and 11. In mid-July, Russia suspended exports through the Don-Azov Canal. Russian wheat exports via the Sea of Azov suffered a further setback following a Ukrainian attack on a major grain export terminal at the Russian port of Taman in late July.

As the saying goes, misfortunes rarely come alone. Attacks on food-related facilities and supply routes involving two of the world’s largest grain producers have coincided with a decline in global wheat production caused by drought and climate change.

According to estimates by the US Department of Agriculture, the combined production of the world’s seven largest wheat-exporting countries is likely to fall by 11 percent in the 2026-27 season.

Together, these developments pose a dual threat to global food security. The capacity to produce food is declining, while the ability to deliver it to importing markets is being disrupted, amid rising transport costs and the growing expense of securing shipments.

Ultimately, the war unfolding in the Black Sea will translate into higher food prices, rising import bills and the depletion of strategic reserves, particularly in Arab and African countries that depend heavily on imported grain.

The disruption of energy supplies caused by the war in Gulf waters is already fuelling inflation. Now, the decline in food supplies resulting from the war in the Black Sea threatens to add another, equally dangerous source of inflation.

articles.title: The Mandarin in Macaulay's exam hall
articles.summary: Rahul Sagar’s recent column in an English daily , marking Thomas Babington Macaulay's 226th birth anniversary, makes a persuasive case that the open
articles.body: Rahul Sagar’s recent column in an English daily , marking Thomas Babington Macaulay's 226th birth anniversary, makes a persuasive case that the open competitive examination, not the much-maligned 1835 Minute on Education, was Macaulay's most consequential legacy in India. His story runs from Lord Grenville's 1813 proposal, through the failings of Haileybury, to the Charter Act of 1853 and the first open competition for the Indian Civil Service in 1855. In this telling, Macaulay's model was Oxford and Cambridge.What the story leaves out is the oldest and best-documented precedent: China.By the time Macaulay rose in Parliament in 1833, the Chinese imperial examination had been selecting officials for more than twelve centuries. Instituted under the Sui dynasty around 605 CE and expanded under the Tang and Song, the keju system tested candidates on the Confucian classics, ranked them, and sent the successful into the bureaucracy. It was the world's first durable answer to the very problem Macaulay faced: how to staff a vast administration with men chosen for learning rather than connections. It lasted until 1905.This was no obscure precedent. From the early seventeenth century, Jesuit accounts, beginning with Matteo Ricci's journals, described China's examination halls to European readers. Enlightenment writers, Voltaire foremost among them, held up the Chinese mandarinate as a rebuke to Europe's hereditary privilege. By the nineteenth century, the Britons who knew China best were explicit. Thomas Taylor Meadows, an interpreter in the British consular service in China, urged in his Desultory Notes on the Government and People of China (1847) that Britain adopt competitive examinations on the Chinese pattern.The route the idea took matters for India. In a classic 1943 study in the Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies, the historian Teng Ssu-yu argued that East India Company men familiar with China carried the examination idea into the Company's reforms, so that competition was tried in India before Britain adopted it at home through the Northcote-Trevelyan Report of 1854. That report's co-author, Charles Trevelyan, was a veteran of the Company's Indian service and Macaulay's own brother-in-law. Opponents in Britain knew where the idea came from; critics derided competitive examination as a "Chinese" innovation, unfit for English gentlemen.None of this diminishes Macaulay's role as an advocate. But it changes the story. The examination that produced the "competition-wallah" was not simply a gift that liberal Britain bestowed on India. It was an Asian institution that reached Britain through its Asian empire, and was then administered to Indians as if it were a European discovery.India, too, had traditions of testing learning, though in different forms. The seventh-century Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang reported that at Nalanda, learned gatekeepers questioned would-be students on arrival, and most were turned away. Shastrartha, the formal public debate, was for centuries the arena in which scholarly reputations were won and lost before royal courts. Kautilya's Arthashastra prescribed secret tests, upadha, to assess ministers' integrity before appointment. These were not civil service examinations in the Chinese sense, but they show that the principle that authority should rest on demonstrated ability was hardly foreign to the subcontinent.There is an irony here. Sagar's own scholarship, most recently The Birth of Indian Liberalism, argues convincingly that Indian liberalism was not merely borrowed from Britain but was an indigenous project with its own ambitions. The same corrective applies to the civil service. To credit merit-based selection to Oxbridge and Macaulay alone is to repeat the derivative narrative Sagar has worked so hard to dismantle elsewhere.Why does this matter now? Every year, hundreds of thousands of young Indians sit the UPSC civil services examination. The debates Sagar notes, over cramming, unequal access, and whether examinations select for wisdom or memory, were rehearsed in China for a thousand years before Britain encountered them. Chinese critics complained that the "eight-legged essay" rewarded formula over thought, and reformers repeatedly tried to balance literary polish with practical statecraft. India's examination system would be better understood, and perhaps better reformed, if we recognized it as heir to an Asian tradition and not only to a Victorian one.Macaulay deserves credit for championing competition. But the idea of merit he championed was older, and more Asian, than either his admirers or his critics usually admit. Remembering that is not a rejection of the liberal inheritance; it is a fuller account of it.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: JACKSON THOMPSON: Father of Michigan volleyball player blasts El-Sayed for '60 Minutes' girls' sports remark
articles.summary: Sean Lechner fires back at Abdul El-Sayed's remarks, saying his daughter's volleyball lawsuit proves transgender sports debates aren't manufactured.
articles.body: The father of a Michigan volleyball player suing over a transgender opponent blasted Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s "60 Minutes" remarks, saying his family’s experience shows the dispute is far from manufactured. "Mr. El-Sayed, how can you look my daughter in the eyes and call this a manufactured issue? She is living this fight," Sean Lechner, father of Monroe High School volleyball player Briley Lechner, said in a statement. "Our entire family has lived it for a year, and it’s a living hell!! it is far from over." MICHIGAN TEEN VOLLEYBALL PLAYER FILES LAWSUIT AFTER SHE UNKNOWINGLY SHARED LOCKER ROOM WITH TRANS ATHLETE Lechner’s response followed an exchange in El-Sayed’s extended interview with Ross Douthat. Douthat asked about parental control over education, including transgender students’ participation on sports teams, and how to resolve situations in which rights conflict. "I don't know that that's actually true," El-Sayed responded. "I think we manufacture these social issues..." El-Sayed argued that smartphones make it unrealistic for parents to prevent children from encountering information they find objectionable. He later said eligibility decisions should belong to sports governing bodies. "I'm not running to govern sports," he said. For the Lechners, the issue has led to federal litigation. Briley and her father filed suit Oct. 9 against Monroe Public Schools, the Michigan High School Athletic Association and district officials. Their attorneys at the Thomas More Law Center allege officials knew before a Sept. 9, 2025, match that Ann Arbor Skyline’s girls’ volleyball team included a transgender athlete, but did not tell Monroe players or parents. The suit also alleges the opposing player was permitted to use the girls’ locker-room facilities without Monroe athletes being informed. MICHIGAN FATHER ALLEGES BOMB THREAT TO HOME AFTER DAUGHTER SPOKE UP ABOUT FACING TRANS ATHLETE WITHOUT KNOWING The district deemed the family’s Title IX allegations unsubstantiated. The lawsuit challenges that determination and the handling of their appeal. "I find your statement disgusting. You undermine female athletes and disrespect families who deserve answers," Lechner said of El-Sayed’s remarks. "My daughter’s privacy, dignity and right to fair competition deserve more than your manufactured, political talking points." El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate election Tuesday. In the interview, El-Sayed argued that culture-war disputes distract from economic concerns, including groceries, gas and access to medical care. Lechner urged voters to put their children ahead of party loyalty. "My faith and my family come first. I pray every Michigander votes for the person, not the party, and demands leaders with the courage to protect our children," he said. India and New Zealand clash in the first of five ODIs in the series at Eden Park, Auckland on Wednesday, November 4.

The Indians won the recent T20I series 3-2 despite the Kiwis managing to win the last two matches. The ODI series will see the comeback of Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli in the Indian squad, while Shubman Gill leads the team in the first three ODIs.

The home side is dealing with some injuries of late as Rachin Ravindra and Mark Chapman are ruled out of the series while Devon Conway misses the first ODI due to a concussion suffered in a training.

The Men in Blue will also hope to better their record in ODIs against New Zealand at Eden Park as they have won only four of their 11 ODIs at the venue against the hosts. Weather might be an important factor in the game.

The Sporting News takes a look at how the weather is expected to behave in Auckland for the first ODI between India and New Zealand.

Auckland weather forecast for New Zealand vs. India 1st ODI

The weather report for Wednesday looks quite promising for the start of the series with showers expected in Auckland in the morning.

According to the current forecast , there is a prediction of a high of about 21°C with temperatures remaining near 20°C at the start of the game. The weather will continue to get brighter throughout the day and partly sunny conditions are predicted.

There is a prediction of temperatures dropping down to about 19°C by evening time.

Hourly weather forecast for New Zealand vs. India 1st ODI

Chances of rain interrupting play in Auckland

There is a 55% chance of rain during the day on Wednesday in Auckland, yet the timing of the rain showers is good news for both teams.

It is anticipated to rain and shower in the morning, with chances of precipitation staying fairly high until about 10 a.m. The chances, however, are anticipated to go down as the afternoon comes closer.

The chances of rain during the playing time will be about 15% per hour at first, but then drop down to the single digits by late afternoon, suggesting no indications of heavy rains during the game.

What happens if the New Zealand vs. India 1st ODI is stopped by rain?

If in any case rain interrupts play, the playing conditions can be adjusted to compensate for the loss of time.

The Duckworth-Lewis-Stern (DLS) system will be applied to set a new target based on a reduction in the number of overs. First, the match officials will try to play as many overs as possible given the weather conditions and playing time.

If it is not viable to bowl enough overs to get a result, the match will end in a no-result match.

Eden Park pitch report and dew factor for IND vs NZ 1st ODI

Traditionally, the playing surface in Eden Park is good for batting due to the flat pitch and shorter straight boundaries which facilitate stroke play for batters once they have got their eye in.

The new ball could provide some help to fast bowlers early on in the game. The spin bowlers are expected to be part of the team during the middle overs.

There is also an aspect of dew on the field that could affect the second innings of the game because while the start time for the game is 3:00 p.m. local time, the later stages will be played when the sun sets over Auckland. This may create favorable conditions due to high humidity.

What time does the New Zealand vs. India 1st ODI start?

The first ODI between New Zealand and India will be played at Eden Park in Auckland, New Zealand.

It is scheduled to start at 3:00 p.m. local time (NZDT), which translates to 7:30 a.m. IST on Wednesday, November 4 , for viewers in India .

articles.title: 50 years after Nepal banned cannabis, SC orders regulated cultivation within 3 months
articles.summary: Fifty years after Nepal banned all cannabis cultivation, Supreme Court has directed govt to frame regulations within three months to allow its controlled
articles.body: Fifty years after Nepal banned all cannabis cultivation, Supreme Court has directed govt to frame regulations within three months to allow its controlled cultivation for medicinal, scientific and industrial purposes, potentially opening the door to a legal cannabis industry in the Himalayan nation. The court held that successive govts had failed to implement provisions of a law enacted in 1976 that already allowed limited cultivation under regulation.The verdict, delivered on May 18, 2025, remained unpublished for nearly 18 months after court records were destroyed in an arson attack during the violent Gen Z protests on Sept 9, 2025. Its full text emerged only last week, bringing renewed attention to a ban Nepal imposed in 1976 under international pressure, particularly from the US.The court criticised successive govts for failing to implement provisions of the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976, which permits certain forms of regulated cultivation and medicinal use. "The failure to do so amounts to a refusal or neglect by govt to discharge its legal obligations," the court observed. It directed authorities to frame rules for licensing and monitoring the cultivation, processing, storage, sale, distribution, import and export of cannabis within three months of receiving the order."It is therefore the duty of state authorities to formulate such rules without delay," the judgment said in a published English translation. The order did not permit recreational use, which remains illegal, and left any wider relaxation of cannabis laws to parliament.The ruling could bring new opportunities for farmers in Nepal's mountainous regions, where cannabis grows naturally and cultivation has continued illegally despite the ban. Campaigners have argued for years that prohibition did little to stop production while denying farmers a source of income. They believe a regulated industry could give growers access to legal markets and create jobs in processing, medicine and other cannabis-based products.Rajiv Kafle, a prominent cannabis legalisation campaigner, has long called for Nepal to replace prohibition with regulation. "In fact, regulation is a better policy option," he told TOI, pointing to the economic opportunities that countries with legal cannabis industries had already begun exploiting.Former health minister Birodh Khatiwada, another advocate of legalisation, has questioned why Nepal continued to criminalise a crop that several other countries had begun permitting. "It is not justifiable that a poor country like ours has to treat cannabis as a drug," he said earlier, criticising the difference between restrictions in developing countries and changing policies in wealthier nations.Saurav Dhakal of Green Growth Nepal has also argued that cannabis cultivation could help rural communities, but warned that large companies should not be allowed to corner the benefits. "We need to make sure that legalising cannabis benefits the neediest Nepalis," he said, calling for small farmers and cooperatives to have a meaningful share in any future legal industry.Nepal has made several attempts to ease its cannabis restrictions, but little has changed on the ground. A parliamentary Bill introduced in 2020 failed to make progress, while a 2024 govt announcement allowing medicinal cannabis cultivation produced few results. Gandaki Province passed legislation in July 2026 permitting regulated cultivation for medicinal and industrial purposes, but federal restrictions continued to complicate its implementation.Grass Roots: How ban came aboutDuring the 1960s and early 1970s, Kathmandu's Freak Street became a prominent stop on the hippie trail, attracting Western backpackers, counterculture travellers and Americans seeking to avoid conscription during the Vietnam War. Govt-licensed shops openly sold marijuana and hashish. As then US President Richard Nixon intensified the 'War on Drugs', Nepal faced mounting pressure to shut down the trade.In 1973, Nepal revoked cannabis trading licences, closing the licensed hashish shops. The Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976, subsequently criminalised cultivation, sale and consumption, although it retained limited exceptions for regulated activities that successive govts failed to implement.Ironically, several US states have legalised recreational marijuana years ago, while Nepal continues to criminalise unauthorised cultivation and consumption.You use AI every day.
